lead: A version control system (VCS) records every change to a project as an immutable snapshot, so any past state can be rebuilt exactly. It exists because software changes many times, by many people, and one wrong edit must not destroy months of work. Teams use it for history, undo, parallel work on branches, release baselines and an audit trail. Git is the common distributed VCS; a push or a tag is also what wakes the CI server.
prereq: You need: the idea of a baseline and change control from Unit 6, Software configuration management, and the test plan vocabulary from 5.1.

blocks.text: A version control system keeps a repository: the full stored history of a project. Your working copy is the set of files you edit on your machine. A commit is one immutable snapshot of the whole project tree, plus metadata: author, time, message and parent commit. A revision is one point in that history. A branch is a movable name that points to a commit; a tag is a fixed name, often used for a release. The mainline (also called trunk or main) is the branch the team treats as the shared line.

Changes are recorded as whole snapshots, not as a patch of each file. Git still stores files efficiently by keeping identical content once and by packing objects. For a reader, the important point is that any commit can rebuild the exact tree.

items: Merge: join two histories into one commit.
Conflict: Git cannot choose between two edits to the same region, so a person decides.
Baseline: a commit used as the fixed reference for a release or a test cycle.
Audit trail: the record of who changed what, when and why, read from commits.

blocks.where: id is the commit name; H is a cryptographic hash such as SHA-1 in classic Git; tree is the root directory snapshot; parents are earlier commits, none for the first commit and two or more for a merge commit; author and message are metadata.

blocks.text: A centralised VCS has one server that holds all history. Your client holds a working copy and asks the server for log, diff or old versions. CVS and Subversion work this way. Backup is in one place, but history needs the network, and branching can be costly.

A distributed VCS gives every clone the full history and all objects. Git and Mercurial work this way. You can log, diff, commit and branch offline. Push sends your commits to another repository; pull brings commits in. Every clone is also a backup.

Git internals at working level: a blob holds file content; a tree holds a directory listing that names blobs and subtrees; a commit points to one root tree and to its parent commits. The commit graph is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Arrows point from a child commit to its parents, and a cycle cannot exist because a commit is named by the hash of its contents, including parent hashes. Editing old history changes later hashes.

blocks.text: A file named .gitignore lists paths Git must not track: build output, logs, editor files and secrets. A hook is a script that runs at a fixed point, such as before a commit or before a push. A pre-commit hook can run a linter or fast tests; a pre-push hook can run a longer check. A failing hook rejects the action.

items: Trunk-based: small commits go to mainline often; short-lived branches are optional.
Feature branch: one branch per feature, merged when tested.
Release branch: frozen for final fixes while mainline moves on.
Keep commits small and messages clear: state what changed and why.
A push or a tag is the event that wakes the CI server; see 5.6 and 5.7.

figure.caption: The feature branch leaves the mainline at B, gains D and E, and merges back at M; M has two parents, C and E. Commit C carries the release tag v1.0.

spec.aria: A commit graph where a feature branch splits from the mainline, gains one commit, and merges back into a merge commit that has two parents.

examples.question: Merge branch feature/pay into main and predict the conflicts. The base commit of app.py has 20 lines. feature/pay inserts 6 lines after line 10 and also changes line 4. main changes line 15 and also changes line 4. How many conflict regions will Git report, how many lines will the merged file have, and how many parents will the merge commit have?
steps: The merge base is the common parent of the two branch tips. Call the feature tip E and the main tip C; the base is B.
Compare C with B: main changes line 4 and line 15.
Compare E with B: feature changes line 4 and inserts 6 lines after base line 10.
The insertion after line 10 and the change at line 15 touch different regions, so Git merges them automatically.
Line 4 changed in both branches, so Git stops on that one region and writes conflict markers there.
The developer edits line 4, runs git add app.py, then git commit. Git creates merge commit M with parents C and E.
Line count: base 20 lines plus 6 inserted lines = 26 lines. Main's line changes do not add or remove lines.
Conflict count: only line 4 overlaps, so there is 1 conflict region. Merge commit parents: 2, namely C and E.
examples.answer: Git reports 1 conflict region, the merged file has 26 lines, and merge commit M has 2 parents.
examples.check:
base = 20
inserted = 6
feature_changed = {4}
main_changed = {4, 15}
conflicts = len(feature_changed & main_changed)
merged_lines = base + inserted
parents = 2
print(conflicts)
print(merged_lines)
print(parents)

traps: A commit stores a snapshot of the whole tree, not a list of per-file differences. Git may store content efficiently, but the model is snapshot plus parent pointer.
Merge and rebase are not the same. Merge creates a commit with two parents; rebase replays commits on a new base and changes their ids.
pull is fetch plus integration. fetch only downloads commits and does not move your branch.
Never commit build output, local config or passwords. Add paths to .gitignore and keep secrets outside the repository.
A branch moves as new commits arrive; a tag stays on one commit. Do not use a branch name as a release baseline.

quiz.q: Define repository, working copy and commit.
quiz.a: A repository is the stored history. A working copy is the set of files you edit. A commit is one immutable snapshot of the whole tree plus metadata and parent pointers.

quiz.q: What is a tag in Git?
quiz.a: A fixed name attached to one commit, often used to mark a release baseline.

quiz.q: Why can a distributed VCS show log and diff while offline?
quiz.a: Every clone holds the full history and all objects, so log and diff read local data and do not need the server.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a pre-commit hook and a pre-push hook?
quiz.a: A pre-commit hook runs before a commit is recorded, so it should be fast. A pre-push hook runs before commits leave the machine, so it can run longer checks. Either can reject the action.

quiz.q: A base file has 30 lines. feature/x inserts 4 lines after line 8. main changes line 20. How many conflict regions, and how many lines in the merged file?
quiz.a: The insertion after line 8 and the change at line 20 are different regions, so there are 0 conflicts. Lines = 30 + 4 = 34 lines.

quiz.q: Write the Git command that creates and switches to a new branch named feature/pay.
quiz.a: git switch -c feature/pay (older Git: git checkout -b feature/pay).

quiz.q: Why is the Git commit graph a DAG, and what would a cycle mean?
quiz.a: Each commit points to earlier parent commits, and its hash includes the parent hashes. A cycle would make a commit its own ancestor and would require changing hashes, so it cannot occur in a valid history.

quiz.q: A team commits the compiled dist folder and a .env file. Explain two risks and the fix.
quiz.a: The repository grows and every build adds noise; the .env file can leak passwords and keys. Fix: add dist and .env to .gitignore, remove them from tracking, and store secrets outside the repository.

beyond: Not for the exam. Git stores objects under .git/objects and packs them into packfiles, which is why a full clone can be smaller than a copy of every version. Newer Git can use SHA-256 object names, and large teams add signed commits, partial clones and monorepo tooling. Search for Git internals, commit graph, trunk-based development, signed commits and partial clone.
